Chapter 4 · Geography · Contemporary India II

Agriculture

Two-thirds of India’s people are engaged in agriculture, which feeds us and supplies raw material to industry. This chapter covers the farming systems of India, the rabi–kharif–zaid cycle, every major crop from rice to jute, and the technological and institutional reforms — including the Green Revolution and Bhoodan–Gramdan.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

India is an agriculturally important country. Two-thirds of its population is engaged in agricultural activities. Agriculture is a primary activity, which produces most of the food that we consume. Besides food grains, it also produces raw material for various industries, and some agricultural products like tea, coffee and spices are also exported.

Cultivation methods have changed significantly depending upon the characteristics of the physical environment, technological know-how and socio-cultural practices. Farming varies from subsistence to commercial type: primitive subsistence farming, intensive subsistence farming, and commercial farming (including plantation agriculture).

The chapter then explains India’s cropping pattern — the three seasons rabi, kharif and zaid — and describes the major crops: rice, wheat, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), maize, pulses, sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, horticultural crops, and the fibre crops cotton, jute, hemp and silk.

It closes with technological and institutional reforms — land reform, the Green Revolution, the White Revolution, crop insurance, Grameen banks, Kisan Credit Card, minimum support price — and the Bhoodan–Gramdan movement of Vinoba Bhave, the “blood-less revolution”.

Share of population

Two-thirds of India’s population is engaged in agricultural activities; over 60 per cent depend on agriculture for livelihood.

Three farming types

Primitive subsistence (slash and burn), intensive subsistence (labour-intensive), commercial (including plantation).

Three cropping seasons

Rabi (sown October–December, harvested April–June), kharif (with the monsoon, harvested September–October), zaid (short summer season).

Rice

Kharif; above 25°C and annual rainfall above 100 cm; India is the second largest producer after China.

Wheat

Rabi; 50–75 cm rainfall; two zones — Ganga–Satluj plains and the black soil region of the Deccan.

Sugarcane

21°C–27°C, 75–100 cm rainfall; India is second largest producer after Brazil.

Tea and coffee

Tea: Assam, Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri; India second after China (2020). Coffee: Arabica from Yemen, Baba Budan Hills, Nilgiri.

Jute

The “golden fibre”; West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya.

Reforms

Land reform in the First Five Year Plan; Green Revolution; White Revolution (Operation Flood); KCC; PAIS; MSP.

Bhoodan–Gramdan

Vinoba Bhave at Pochampally, Telangana; Ram Chandra Reddy offered 80 acres to 80 landless villagers.

Agriculture in India

India is an agriculturally important country. Two-thirds of its population is engaged in agricultural activities. Agriculture is a primary activity, which produces most of the food that we consume. Besides food grains, it also produces raw material for various industries, and some agricultural products like tea, coffee and spices are also exported.

Agriculture has been practised in India for thousands of years. Sustained use of land without compatible techno-institutional changes has hindered the pace of agricultural development. Despite the development of sources of irrigation, most farmers in large parts of the country still depend upon monsoon and natural fertility to carry on their agriculture. For a growing population this poses a serious challenge. Agriculture provides livelihood for more than 60 per cent of the population and needs serious technical and institutional reforms.

Do it yourself

Can you name some industries based on agricultural raw material?

Types of Farming

Agriculture is an age-old economic activity in our country. Over these years, cultivation methods have changed significantly depending upon the characteristics of the physical environment, technological know-how and socio-cultural practices. Farming varies from subsistence to commercial type. At present, in different parts of India, the following farming systems are practised.

Primitive Subsistence Farming

This type of farming is still practised in a few pockets of India. Primitive subsistence agriculture is practised on small patches of land with the help of primitive tools like hoe, dao and digging sticks, and family/community labour. This type of farming depends upon monsoon, natural fertility of the soil and suitability of other environmental conditions to the crops grown.

It is a “slash and burn” agriculture. Farmers clear a patch of land and produce cereals and other food crops to sustain their family. When soil fertility decreases, the farmers shift and clear a fresh patch of land for cultivation. This type of shifting allows Nature to replenish the fertility of the soil through natural processes; land productivity in this type of agriculture is low as the farmer does not use fertilisers or other modern inputs. It is known by different names in different parts of the country.

Intensive Subsistence Farming

This type of farming is practised in areas of high population pressure on land. It is labour-intensive farming, where high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation are used for obtaining higher production.

Though the “right of inheritance” leading to the division of land among successive generations has rendered land-holding size uneconomical, farmers continue to take maximum output from the limited land in the absence of alternative sources of livelihood. Thus there is enormous pressure on agricultural land.

Do it yourself

Can you name some of the states of India where such farming is practised?

Commercial Farming

The main characteristic of this type of farming is the use of higher doses of modern inputs, e.g. high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides, in order to obtain higher productivity. The degree of commercialisation of agriculture varies from one region to another. For example, rice is a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab, but in Odisha it is a subsistence crop.

Plantation

Plantation is also a type of commercial farming. In this type of farming, a single crop is grown on a large area. The plantation has an interface of agriculture and industry. Plantations cover large tracts of land, using capital-intensive inputs, with the help of migrant labourers. All the produce is used as raw material in respective industries.

In India, tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana, etc., are important plantation crops. Tea in Assam and North Bengal, coffee in Karnataka, are some of the important plantation crops grown in these states. Since the production is mainly for market, a well-developed network of transport and communication connecting the plantation areas, processing industries and markets plays an important role in the development of plantations.

Can you give some more examples of crops which may be commercial in one region and may provide subsistence in another region?

Case study: Rinjha’s family

Rinjha lived with her family in a small village at the outskirts of Diphu in Assam. She enjoys watching her family members clearing, slashing and burning a patch of land for cultivation. She often helps them in irrigating the fields with water running through a bamboo canal from the nearby spring. She loves the surroundings and wants to stay here as long as she can, but this little girl has no idea about the declining fertility of the soil and her family’s search for a fresh patch of land in the next season.

Do it yourself

Can you name the type of farming Rinjha’s family is engaged in? Can you enlist some crops which are grown in such farming?

Teacher explanation

Answer: Rinjha’s family practises primitive subsistence (slash and burn) farming — called jhumming in Assam. Such fields grow cereals and other food crops for the family: rice, maize, millets, pulses, and vegetables such as pumpkin and chillies. The declining fertility and the search for a fresh patch are exactly what the chapter describes.

Cropping Pattern

India has three cropping seasons — rabi, kharif and zaid. Various types of food and fibre crops, vegetables and fruits, spices and condiments, etc., constitute some of the important crops grown in the country.

The three cropping seasons of India
SeasonSowingHarvestingImportant crops
RabiWinter, from October to DecemberSummer, from April to JuneWheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard
KharifWith the onset of the monsoonSeptember–OctoberPaddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean
ZaidShort season during the summer months, between rabi and kharifBefore the monsoonWatermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops

Rabi crops

Rabi crops are sown in winter from October to December and harvested in summer from April to June. Important rabi crops are wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. Though these crops are grown in large parts of India, states from the north and north-western parts such as Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh are important for the production of wheat and other rabi crops. Availability of precipitation during winter months due to the western temperate cyclones helps in the success of these crops. However, the success of the Green Revolution in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan has also been an important factor in the growth of these rabi crops.

Kharif crops

Kharif crops are grown with the onset of the monsoon in different parts of the country and are harvested in September–October. Important crops are paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean. Some of the most important rice-growing regions are Assam, West Bengal, coastal regions of Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Maharashtra, particularly the Konkan coast, along with Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Recently, paddy has also become an important crop of Punjab and Haryana. In states like Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, three crops of paddy are grown in a year — Aus, Aman and Boro.

Zaid crops

In between the rabi and the kharif seasons, there is a short season during the summer months known as the zaid season. Some of the crops produced during zaid are watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops. Sugarcane takes almost a year to grow.

Major Crops

A variety of food and non-food crops are grown in different parts of the country depending upon the variations in soil, climate and cultivation practices. Major crops grown in India are rice, wheat, millets, pulses, tea, coffee, sugarcane, oilseeds, cotton and jute, etc.

Rice

Rice is the staple food crop of a majority of the people in India. Our country is the second largest producer of rice in the world after China. It is a kharif crop which requires high temperature (above 25°C) and high humidity with annual rainfall above 100 cm. In areas of less rainfall it grows with the help of irrigation.

Rice is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas and the deltaic regions. Development of a dense network of canal irrigation and tube-wells has made it possible to grow rice in areas of less rainfall such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.

Wheat

This is the second most important cereal crop. It is the main food crop in the north and north-western part of the country. This rabi crop requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of ripening. It requires 50 to 75 cm of annual rainfall, evenly distributed over the growing season.

There are two important wheat-growing zones in the country — the Ganga–Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan. The major wheat-producing states are Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan.

Millets

Jowar, bajra and ragi are the important millets grown in India. Though these are known as coarse grains, they have very high nutritional value. For example, ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro-nutrients and roughage.

Jowar is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production. It is a rain-fed crop mostly grown in the moist areas which hardly needs irrigation. Major jowar producing states are Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.

Bajra grows well on sandy soils and shallow black soil. Major bajra producing states are Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Haryana.

Ragi is a crop of dry regions and grows well on red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils. Major ragi producing states are Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Jharkhand and Arunachal Pradesh.

Maize

Maize is a crop which is used both as food and fodder. It is a kharif crop which requires a temperature between 21°C to 27°C and grows well in old alluvial soil. In some states like Bihar, maize is grown in the rabi season also. Use of modern inputs such as HYV seeds, fertilisers and irrigation has contributed to increasing production. Major maize-producing states are Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

Pulses

India is the largest producer as well as the consumer of pulses in the world. These are the major source of protein in a vegetarian diet. Major pulses grown in India are tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram.

Pulses need less moisture and survive even in dry conditions. Being leguminous crops, all these crops except arhar help in restoring soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air. Therefore these are mostly grown in rotation with other crops. Major pulse producing states are Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka.

Sugarcane

It is a tropical as well as subtropical crop. It grows well in a hot and humid climate with a temperature of 21°C to 27°C and an annual rainfall between 75 cm and 100 cm. Irrigation is required in regions of low rainfall. It can be grown on a variety of soils and needs manual labour from sowing to harvesting.

India is the second largest producer of sugarcane only after Brazil. It is the main source of sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses. The major sugarcane-producing states are Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab and Haryana.

Oil Seeds

In 2020 India was the second largest producer of groundnut in the world after China. Different oil seeds are grown covering approximately 12 per cent of the total cropped area of the country. Main oil-seeds produced in India are groundnut, mustard, coconut, sesamum (til), soyabean, castor seeds, cotton seeds, linseed and sunflower. Most of these are edible and used as cooking mediums; however, some are also used as raw material in the production of soap, cosmetics and ointments.

Groundnut is a kharif crop and accounts for about half of the major oilseeds produced in the country. Gujarat was the largest producer of groundnut, followed by Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, in 2019–20. Linseed and mustard are rabi crops. Sesamum is a kharif crop in the north and a rabi crop in south India. Castor seed is grown both as rabi and kharif crop.

Tea

Tea cultivation is an example of plantation agriculture. It is also an important beverage crop introduced in India initially by the British. Today, most of the tea plantations are owned by Indians. The tea plant grows well in tropical and subtropical climates endowed with deep and fertile well-drained soil, rich in humus and organic matter. Tea bushes require warm and moist frost-free climate all through the year; frequent showers evenly distributed over the year ensure continuous growth of tender leaves.

Tea is a labour-intensive industry. It requires abundant, cheap and skilled labour. Tea is processed within the tea garden to restore its freshness. Major tea-producing states are Assam, the hills of Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri districts (West Bengal), Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Apart from these, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Andhra Pradesh and Tripura are also tea-producing states. In 2020 India was the second largest producer of tea after China.

Coffee

Indian coffee is known in the world for its good quality. The Arabica variety initially brought from Yemen is produced in the country. This variety is in great demand all over the world. Initially its cultivation was introduced on the Baba Budan Hills, and even today its cultivation is confined to the Nilgiri in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

Horticulture Crops

In 2020, India was the second largest producer of fruits and vegetables in the world after China. India is a producer of tropical as well as temperate fruits.

  • Mangoes of Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal
  • Oranges of Nagpur and Cherrapunjee (Meghalaya)
  • Bananas of Kerala, Mizoram, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu
  • Lichi and guava of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar
  • Pineapples of Meghalaya
  • Grapes of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra
  • Apples, pears, apricots and walnuts of Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh

These are in great demand the world over. India is an important producer of pea, cauliflower, onion, cabbage, tomato, brinjal and potato.

Fibre Crops

Cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk are the four major fibre crops grown in India. The first three are derived from the crops grown in the soil; the latter is obtained from cocoons of the silkworms fed on green leaves, specially mulberry. Rearing of silkworms for the production of silk fibre is known as sericulture.

Cotton

India is believed to be the original home of the cotton plant. Cotton is one of the main raw materials for the cotton textile industry. India is the second largest producer of cotton after China. Cotton grows well in the drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau. It requires high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine for its growth. It is a kharif crop and requires 6 to 8 months to mature. Major cotton-producing states are Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

Jute

Jute is known as the “golden fibre”. Jute grows well on well-drained fertile soils in the flood plains where soils are renewed every year. High temperature is required during the time of growth. West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya are the major jute producing states. It is used in making gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn, carpets and other artefacts.

Technological and Institutional Reforms

Agriculture has been practised in India for thousands of years. Sustained use of land without compatible techno-institutional changes has hindered the pace of agricultural development. In spite of the development of sources of irrigation, most farmers in large parts of the country still depend upon monsoon and natural fertility in order to carry on their agriculture. For a growing population this poses a serious challenge. Agriculture, which provides livelihood for more than 60 per cent of its population, needs serious technical and institutional reforms.

Thus collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari, etc., were given priority to bring about institutional reforms in the country after Independence. “Land reform” was the main focus of our First Five Year Plan. The right of inheritance had already led to fragmentation of land holdings, necessitating consolidation of holdings.

The laws of land reforms were enacted, but implementation was lacking or lukewarm. The Government of India embarked upon introducing agricultural reforms to improve Indian agriculture in the 1960s and 1970s. The Green Revolution based on the use of package technology and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were some of the strategies initiated to improve the lot of Indian agriculture. But this too led to the concentration of development in a few selected areas.

Therefore, in the 1980s and 1990s, a comprehensive land development programme was initiated, which included both institutional and technical reforms. Provision for crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease, establishment of Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks for providing loan facilities to farmers at lower rates of interest were some important steps in this direction.

Kisan Credit Card (KCC) and the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS) are some other schemes introduced by the Government of India for the benefit of farmers. Moreover, special weather bulletins and agricultural programmes for farmers were introduced on the radio and television. The government also announces minimum support price, remunerative and procurement prices for important crops to check the exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen.

Box: Bhoodan — Gramdan

Mahatma Gandhi declared Vinoba Bhave as his spiritual heir. He also participated in Satyagraha as one of the foremost satyagrahis. He was one of the votaries of Gandhi’s concept of gram swarajya. After Gandhiji’s martyrdom, Vinoba Bhave undertook a padyatra to spread Gandhiji’s message, covering almost the entire country.

Once, when he was delivering a lecture at Pochampally in Telangana, some poor landless villagers demanded some land for their economic well-being. Vinoba Bhave could not promise it to them immediately but assured them that he would talk to the Government of India regarding provision of land for them if they undertook cooperative farming. Suddenly, Shri Ram Chandra Reddy stood up and offered 80 acres of land to be distributed among 80 landless villagers. This act was known as “Bhoodan”.

Later he travelled and introduced his ideas widely all over India. Some zamindars, owners of many villages, offered to distribute some villages among the landless. It was known as Gramdan. However, many landowners chose to provide some part of their land to the poor farmers due to the fear of the land ceiling act. This Bhoodan–Gramdan movement initiated by Vinoba Bhave is also known as the Blood-less Revolution.

Key Terms and Definitions

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
AgricultureA primary activity that produces most of the food we consume and raw material for industries; two-thirds of India’s population is engaged in it.
Primitive subsistence farmingFarming on small patches with primitive tools such as hoe, dao and digging sticks, using family or community labour; also called slash and burn agriculture.
Slash and burn agricultureClearing a patch of land by cutting and burning vegetation, cropping it until fertility falls, then shifting to a fresh patch — jhumming in India’s north-east.
JhummingThe name for slash and burn cultivation in the north-eastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland) and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Intensive subsistence farmingLabour-intensive farming in areas of high population pressure on land, using high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation.
Commercial farmingFarming with higher doses of modern inputs — HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides — to obtain higher productivity.
PlantationA type of commercial farming in which a single crop is grown over a large area with capital-intensive inputs and migrant labour; the produce is used as raw material in industry.
HYV seedsHigh-yielding variety seeds used in commercial farming to raise productivity.
Cropping patternThe arrangement of crops through the year in the three seasons rabi, kharif and zaid.
Rabi seasonWinter season — crops sown October to December and harvested April to June (wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard).
Kharif seasonCrops grown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October (paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, cotton, jute, groundnut).
Zaid seasonA short summer season between rabi and kharif — watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder.
Aus, Aman and BoroThe three paddy crops grown in a year in Assam, West Bengal and Odisha.
MilletsCoarse grains of high nutritional value — jowar, bajra and ragi; ragi is rich in iron, calcium, micro-nutrients and roughage.
Leguminous cropsCrops such as pulses that fix nitrogen from the air and restore soil fertility; all pulses except arhar do this.
SericultureRearing of silkworms for the production of silk fibre.
Golden fibreJute — grown on well-drained fertile soils of flood plains, used for gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn and carpets.
HorticultureCultivation of fruits and vegetables; India was the second largest producer of fruits and vegetables in the world in 2020.
Green RevolutionThe strategy of using package technology — HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation — to raise foodgrain production, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
White RevolutionOperation Flood — the strategy to improve milk production and the lot of Indian agriculture.
Land reformInstitutional reforms such as collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari; the main focus of the First Five Year Plan.
Kisan Credit CardA government scheme giving farmers easy credit for agricultural needs.
MSPMinimum support price — announced by the government for important crops to check exploitation by speculators and middlemen.
BhoodanA voluntary gift of land for the landless; began when Ram Chandra Reddy offered 80 acres to 80 landless villagers at Pochampally.
GramdanGift of whole villages by zamindars to the landless, as part of Vinoba Bhave’s movement.
Blood-less RevolutionAnother name for the Bhoodan–Gramdan movement initiated by Vinoba Bhave.

MaizeKharif (rabi in Bihar)21–27°C, old alluvial soilKarnataka, MP, UP, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana
PulsesKharif and rabiLess moisture, survive dry conditions; fix nitrogenMP, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, UP, Karnataka
SugarcaneAlmost a year21–27°C, 75–100 cm rainfall, any soil, manual labourUP, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana
TeaPlantationDeep fertile well-drained soil rich in humus; warm moist frost-free climateAssam, Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri (WB), Tamil Nadu, Kerala
CoffeePlantationArabica variety from Yemen; confined to the NilgiriKarnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu
CottonKharifDrier parts of black cotton soil, high temperature, light rainfall, 210 frost-free daysMaharashtra, Gujarat, MP, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana, UP
JuteKharifWell-drained fertile flood-plain soils renewed every year; high temperatureWest Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya

07

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Can you name some industries based on agricultural raw material?

Model answer

Cotton textile and jute textile industries (fibre), sugar industry (sugarcane), oil and vanaspati (oilseeds), tea and coffee processing, food processing and flour mills (wheat, rice), rubber, paper (bamboo and wood), and sericulture-based silk industry.

2.

Can you name some such types of farming? (other than the ones described)

Model answer

The chapter itself names jhumming, Pamlou, Dipa, Bewar/Dahiya, Podu/Penda, Pama Dabi/Koman/Bringa, Kumari, Valre/Waltre, Khil and Kuruwa in India, and Milpa, Conuco, Roca, Masole, Ladang and Ray abroad — all forms of slash and burn farming.

3.

Can you enlist some crops which are grown in such farming? (primitive subsistence)

Model answer

Cereals and other food crops for the family — rice, maize, millets such as jowar and bajra, pulses, and vegetables and tubers. Rinjha’s family in Assam grows such food crops after clearing, slashing and burning a patch.

4.

Can you name some of the states of India where intensive subsistence farming is practised?

Model answer

States with high population pressure on land, such as West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala and the deltaic regions of the east coast, where small holdings are farmed with high doses of inputs and irrigation.

5.

Can you give some more examples of crops which may be commercial in one region and may provide subsistence in another region?

Model answer

Rice is commercial in Haryana and Punjab but a subsistence crop in Odisha. Similarly, wheat is commercial in Punjab and Haryana but largely subsistence in parts of Bihar and eastern India, and sugarcane is a commercial crop in western Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra but grown for gur locally in many areas.

6.

Can you name the type of farming Rinjha’s family is engaged in? Can you enlist some crops which are grown in such farming?

Model answer

Primitive subsistence farming — slash and burn agriculture, called jhumming in Assam. They clear, slash and burn a patch, irrigate with water from a bamboo canal, and grow cereals and other food crops to sustain the family.

7.

Can you distinguish which of these pulses are grown in the kharif season and which are grown in the rabi season?

Model answer

Tur (arhar) and urad and moong are kharif pulses; gram, peas and masur (lentil) are rabi pulses. The chapter notes that pulses need less moisture and that all of them except arhar fix nitrogen.

8.

List the items which are made of rubber and are used by us.

Model answer

Tyres and tubes, footwear, hoses, belts, gaskets, erasers, gloves, mattresses, balloons, insulation, sports goods and medical items. Rubber is an important industrial raw material grown mainly in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Garo hills of Meghalaya.

9.

Collect information about agriculture, horticulture and agricultural schemes from the Farmers’ Portal website and discuss the benefits.

Model answer

The portal brings together information on crops, horticulture, schemes, credit, insurance, market prices and advisory services in one place, so a farmer can find the nearest soil-testing laboratory, scheme eligibility, mandi prices and weather advice. The benefit is informed decision-making and access to support without visiting many offices. (Student answers will vary.)

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following describes a system of agriculture where a single crop is grown on a large area? (a) Shifting agriculture (b) Plantation agriculture (c) Horticulture (d) Intensive agriculture

Model answer

(b) Plantation agriculture. A plantation grows a single crop on a large area with capital-intensive inputs and migrant labour, and its produce is used as raw material in industry.

2.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following is a rabi crop? (a) Rice (b) Gram (c) Millets (d) Cotton

Model answer

(b) Gram. Rabi crops are sown October–December and harvested April–June: wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard.

3.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following is a leguminous crop? (a) Pulses (b) Jowar (c) Millets (d) Sesamum

Model answer

(a) Pulses. Being leguminous, all pulses except arhar help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air.

4.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Name one important beverage crop and specify the geographical conditions required for its growth. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Tea. It needs a tropical or subtropical climate, deep fertile well-drained soil rich in humus and organic matter, a warm moist frost-free climate all year, and frequent evenly distributed showers.

5.
NCERT exercise2 marks

Name one staple crop of India and the regions where it is produced. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Rice — the staple food of a majority of Indians. It is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas and deltaic regions, and with irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

6.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Enlist the various institutional reform programmes introduced by the government in the interest of farmers. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation, abolition of zamindari, land reform under the First Five Year Plan, crop insurance, Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks, Kisan Credit Card, PAIS, weather bulletins and minimum support prices.

7.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Suggest the initiative taken by the government to ensure the increase in agricultural production. (about 120 words)

Model answer

After Independence the government gave priority to institutional reforms — collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari — with land reform as the main focus of the First Five Year Plan, because the right of inheritance had fragmented holdings. In the 1960s and 1970s it introduced the Green Revolution based on package technology and the White Revolution (Operation Flood). Since these concentrated development in a few areas, the 1980s and 1990s saw a comprehensive land development programme with both institutional and technical reforms: crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease; Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks giving loans at lower interest; the Kisan Credit Card and Personal Accident Insurance Scheme; special weather bulletins and agricultural programmes on radio and television; and announcement of minimum support, remunerative and procurement prices to check exploitation by speculators and middlemen.

8.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Describe the geographical conditions required for the growth of rice. (about 120 words)

Model answer

Rice is a kharif crop, grown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October. It requires high temperature — above 25°C — and high humidity, with annual rainfall above 100 cm. In areas of less rainfall it can be grown with the help of irrigation, and a dense network of canal irrigation and tube-wells has made this possible in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan. It is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, in coastal areas and in the deltaic regions. Assam, West Bengal, coastal Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, along with Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, are important rice-growing regions, and in Assam, West Bengal and Odisha three crops of paddy — Aus, Aman and Boro — are grown in a year. India is the second largest producer of rice in the world after China.

9.
NCERT projectProject

Project work — Group discussion on the necessity of literacy among farmers.

Model answer

Points for discussion: literacy helps farmers read weather bulletins, scheme notices, seed and fertiliser labels, loan and insurance documents, and mandi prices; it improves bargaining with traders and middlemen; it enables use of the Farmers’ Portal and mobile advisories; and it supports adoption of new technology and better accounting. (Student answers will vary.)

10.
NCERT projectMap

Project work — On an outline map of India, show wheat producing areas.

Model answer

Mark Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan; the two wheat zones are the Ganga–Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Distinguish between primitive subsistence farming and commercial farming. (5 marks)

Model answer

Primitive subsistence: practised on small patches with primitive tools — hoe, dao and digging sticks — and family or community labour; depends on monsoon, natural fertility and suitability of environmental conditions; it is slash and burn agriculture in which farmers shift when fertility falls; productivity is low because no fertilisers or modern inputs are used; known as jhumming, Podu, Bewar, Kumari, etc. Commercial: uses higher doses of modern inputs — HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides — for higher productivity; the degree of commercialisation varies by region (rice is commercial in Punjab and Haryana but subsistence in Odisha); plantation is a type of commercial farming with a single crop on a large area, capital-intensive inputs, migrant labour and produce used as industrial raw material.

2.

What is plantation agriculture? Give two examples. (3 marks)

Model answer

Plantation is a type of commercial farming in which a single crop is grown on a large area; it has an interface of agriculture and industry, uses capital-intensive inputs and migrant labour, and all the produce is used as raw material in the respective industries. Because production is mainly for the market, transport and communication linking plantations, processing industries and markets are important. Examples: tea in Assam and North Bengal, coffee in Karnataka; also rubber, sugarcane and banana.

3.

Explain the three cropping seasons of India. (5 marks)

Model answer

Rabi: sown in winter from October to December and harvested in summer from April to June — wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard; important in Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh; winter precipitation from western temperate cyclones helps, and the Green Revolution boosted these crops. Kharif: grown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October — paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean. Zaid: a short summer season between rabi and kharif — watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops. Sugarcane takes almost a year to grow.

4.

Describe the geographical conditions required for the growth of wheat and name the wheat-growing zones. (3 marks)

Model answer

Wheat is a rabi crop requiring a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of ripening, with 50–75 cm of annual rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season. The two important wheat-growing zones are the Ganga–Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan. Major producing states are Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan.

5.

Write a note on millets. (5 marks)

Model answer

Jowar, bajra and ragi are the important millets. Though called coarse grains, they have very high nutritional value — ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro-nutrients and roughage. Jowar is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production; it is a rain-fed crop grown in moist areas that hardly needs irrigation, mainly in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Bajra grows well on sandy soils and shallow black soil, mainly in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Haryana. Ragi is a crop of dry regions and grows well on red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils, mainly in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Jharkhand and Arunachal Pradesh.

6.

Why are pulses important in Indian agriculture? (3 marks)

Model answer

India is the largest producer and consumer of pulses in the world, and they are the major source of protein in a vegetarian diet. They need less moisture and survive even in dry conditions. Being leguminous, all of them except arhar help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, so they are mostly grown in rotation with other crops. Major producing states are Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka.

7.

Describe the conditions required for cotton and jute. (5 marks)

Model answer

Cotton: India is believed to be the original home of the cotton plant and is the second largest producer after China. It grows well in the drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau and requires high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine; it is a kharif crop requiring 6 to 8 months to mature. Major producers: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh. Jute: known as the golden fibre, it grows well on well-drained fertile soils in flood plains where soils are renewed every year, and requires high temperature during growth. West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya are the major producers; it is used for gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn, carpets and other artefacts.

8.

What is sericulture? Name the four major fibre crops. (2 marks)

Model answer

Sericulture is the rearing of silkworms for the production of silk fibre. The four major fibre crops grown in India are cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk — the first three from crops grown in the soil, the last from cocoons of silkworms fed on mulberry leaves.

9.

Explain the institutional reforms introduced in Indian agriculture after Independence. (5 marks)

Model answer

Collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari were given priority; “land reform” was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan, since the right of inheritance had fragmented holdings. Implementation, however, was lacking or lukewarm. In the 1960s and 1970s the Green Revolution (package technology) and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were introduced, but development concentrated in a few areas. Hence in the 1980s and 1990s a comprehensive land development programme combined institutional and technical reforms: crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease; Grameen banks and cooperative societies and banks giving loans at lower interest; KCC and PAIS; weather bulletins and farm programmes on radio and TV; and minimum support, remunerative and procurement prices to check exploitation by speculators and middlemen.

10.

What was the Bhoodan–Gramdan movement? (3 marks)

Model answer

After Gandhiji’s martyrdom, Vinoba Bhave — whom Gandhiji had declared his spiritual heir — undertook a padyatra across India. At Pochampally in Telangana, poor landless villagers demanded land; Shri Ram Chandra Reddy stood up and offered 80 acres to be distributed among 80 landless villagers. This act was known as Bhoodan. Later, some zamindars offered to distribute whole villages among the landless, which was called Gramdan. Many landowners gave land partly out of fear of the land ceiling act. The movement is also called the Blood-less Revolution.

11.

Why is the Green Revolution criticised even though it raised production? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because it led to the concentration of development in a few selected areas, such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, leaving other regions behind.

12.

Why does India need technical and institutional reform in agriculture? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because sustained use of land without compatible techno-institutional changes has hindered agricultural development; most farmers still depend on the monsoon and natural fertility despite irrigation development; and agriculture supports more than 60 per cent of the population, so a growing population poses a serious challenge.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Why is rice a commercial crop in Punjab and Haryana but a subsistence crop in Odisha? (CBSE pattern, 2 marks)

Model answer

Because the degree of commercialisation varies from region to region. In Punjab and Haryana, irrigation, HYV seeds and modern inputs allow surplus production for the market, while in Odisha rice is largely grown to feed the farmer’s family.

2.
CBSE pattern

Explain any three features of primitive subsistence farming. (3 marks)

Model answer

(i) It is practised on small patches of land with primitive tools such as hoe, dao and digging sticks and family or community labour. (ii) It depends on the monsoon, natural soil fertility and suitability of environmental conditions. (iii) It is slash and burn agriculture: farmers clear a patch, crop it, and shift when fertility falls, so productivity is low as no fertilisers or modern inputs are used.

3.
CBSE pattern

What is the difference between kharif and rabi seasons? (2 marks)

Model answer

Kharif crops are grown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October (paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean). Rabi crops are sown in winter from October to December and harvested in summer from April to June (wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard).

4.
CBSE pattern

Why is tea a labour-intensive industry? (2 marks)

Model answer

Because tea requires abundant, cheap and skilled labour for plucking and processing, and it is processed within the tea garden to restore its freshness.

5.
CBSE pattern

Mention the two important wheat-growing zones of India. (2 marks)

Model answer

The Ganga–Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.

6.
CBSE pattern

Which crop is known as the golden fibre and why? (2 marks)

Model answer

Jute. It is called the golden fibre because of its golden colour and its high value as a fibre used in gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn, carpets and other artefacts.

7.
CBSE pattern

Explain the role of the Kisan Credit Card and PAIS. (2 marks)

Model answer

Both are schemes introduced by the Government of India for the benefit of farmers: the Kisan Credit Card provides easy credit, and the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme gives insurance cover, reducing the risk of farming.

8.
CBSE pattern

Why does the government announce minimum support prices? (2 marks)

Model answer

To check the exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen, by guaranteeing remunerative and procurement prices for important crops.

9.
CBSE pattern

Name the three paddy crops grown in a year in Assam, West Bengal and Odisha. (1 mark)

Model answer

Aus, Aman and Boro.

10.
CBSE pattern

Which states are the major producers of sugarcane? (2 marks)

Model answer

Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab and Haryana.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is agriculture a primary, secondary or tertiary activity?

Model answer

It is a primary activity — it uses the land and natural resources to produce food and raw material.

2.

What is the difference between subsistence and commercial farming?

Model answer

Subsistence farming produces mainly for the farmer’s family, with low inputs and low productivity; commercial farming uses HYV seeds, fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides for higher productivity and produces for the market.

3.

Is maize a food crop or a fodder crop?

Model answer

Both — maize is used as food as well as fodder.

4.

Why is ragi considered nutritious?

Model answer

Because ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro-nutrients and roughage.

5.

Which pulse does not fix nitrogen?

Model answer

Arhar (tur) — the chapter says all pulses except arhar help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen.

6.

Is coffee grown all over India?

Model answer

No. Cultivation is confined to the Nilgiri in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the Arabica variety was initially brought from Yemen and introduced on the Baba Budan Hills.

7.

What is Operation Flood?

Model answer

It is the White Revolution — a strategy initiated along with the Green Revolution to improve Indian agriculture, particularly milk production.

8.

Why is the Bhoodan–Gramdan movement called the blood-less revolution?

Model answer

Because land was redistributed voluntarily — through gifts of land (Bhoodan) and of whole villages (Gramdan) — instead of through violent struggle.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Agriculture is a primary activity.
Reason (R): It produces most of the food we consume and raw material for industries.

2.

Assertion (A): Primitive subsistence farming has low productivity.
Reason (R): The farmer does not use fertilisers or other modern inputs.

3.

Assertion (A): Rice is a kharif crop.
Reason (R): It requires high temperature above 25°C and annual rainfall above 100 cm.

4.

Assertion (A): Pulses help restore soil fertility.
Reason (R): Being leguminous, all pulses except arhar fix nitrogen from the air.

5.

Assertion (A): Tea is grown in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
Reason (R): Tea requires a warm and moist frost-free climate all through the year.

6.

Assertion (A): India is the second largest producer of sugarcane.
Reason (R): Brazil is the largest producer of sugarcane.

7.

Assertion (A): The Green Revolution concentrated development in a few areas.
Reason (R): Therefore a comprehensive land development programme was initiated in the 1980s and 1990s.

8.

Assertion (A): Cotton is grown on black soil of the Deccan plateau.
Reason (R): Cotton requires 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine.

9.

Assertion (A): Jute is called the golden fibre.
Reason (R): It is used in making gunny bags, mats, ropes, yarn and carpets.

10.

Assertion (A): Plantation agriculture is a type of commercial farming.
Reason (R): A single crop is grown on a large area using capital-intensive inputs and migrant labour.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Rinjha’s family (case study)

Case study

Rinjha lived with her family in a small village at the outskirts of Diphu in Assam. She enjoys watching her family members clearing, slashing and burning a patch of land for cultivation. She often helps them in irrigating the fields with water running through a bamboo canal from the nearby spring. She loves the surroundings and wants to stay here as long as she can, but this little girl has no idea about the declining fertility of the soil and her family’s search for a fresh patch of land in the next season.

1.

Which type of farming is Rinjha’s family practising?

Model answer

Primitive subsistence farming — slash and burn agriculture, called jhumming in Assam.

2.

What two features of this farming can you identify from the passage?

Model answer

(i) Clearing, slashing and burning a patch of land; (ii) shifting to a fresh patch when fertility declines. It also uses simple irrigation — a bamboo canal from a spring.

3.

Why is productivity low in this system?

Model answer

Because no fertilisers or modern inputs are used; the farmer depends on the monsoon and natural soil fertility, and must move on when fertility falls.

Source 2 — Data: cropping seasons

Data interpretation
Sowing and harvesting months by season
SeasonSowingHarvesting
RabiOctober–DecemberApril–June
KharifWith the onset of the monsoonSeptember–October
ZaidSummer months (between rabi and kharif)Before the monsoon

How to read this table: the seasons follow one another through the agricultural year, so the same field can carry two or three crops.

1.

Which season has the longest gap between sowing and harvesting?

Model answer

Rabi — sown October to December and harvested April to June, about six months.

2.

Why can three crops be grown on the same land in a year?

Model answer

Because the seasons fit into one agricultural year: kharif in the monsoon, rabi in winter, and a short zaid crop in between. In Assam, West Bengal and Odisha even three paddy crops — Aus, Aman and Boro — are grown.

3.

Which crop takes almost a full year to grow?

Model answer

Sugarcane.

Source 3 — Bhoodan and the land ceiling

Source extract

Vinoba Bhave could not promise land to the landless villagers of Pochampally immediately, but assured them he would talk to the Government of India about provision of land if they undertook cooperative farming. Suddenly Shri Ram Chandra Reddy stood up and offered 80 acres of land to be distributed among 80 landless villagers. This act was known as Bhoodan. Later, some zamindars, owners of many villages, offered to distribute some villages among the landless — known as Gramdan. However, many landowners chose to provide some part of their land to the poor farmers due to the fear of the land ceiling act.

1.

What condition did Vinoba Bhave attach to government help with land?

Model answer

That the villagers should undertake cooperative farming.

2.

What is the difference between Bhoodan and Gramdan?

Model answer

Bhoodan is a gift of land (80 acres at Pochampally) to be distributed among the landless; Gramdan is the gift of whole villages by zamindars who owned many villages.

3.

Why did some landowners give land even without conviction?

Model answer

Because of the fear of the land ceiling act, which limited the land a person could hold.

Mark the main rice-growing regions.

Model answer

Assam, West Bengal, coastal Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, and irrigated Punjab and Haryana.

3.

Locate the tea-producing states.

Model answer

Assam, West Bengal (Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri hills), Tamil Nadu and Kerala; also Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Andhra Pradesh and Tripura.

4.

Mark the coffee-growing region.

Model answer

The Nilgiri in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; introduced on the Baba Budan Hills.

5.

Shade the jute-producing states.

Model answer

West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya.

6.

Mark the cotton belt.

Model answer

The drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau — Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, and also Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.

7.

Locate Pochampally and Diphu.

Model answer

Pochampally in Telangana (where Bhoodan began); Diphu in Assam (Rinjha’s village).

17

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

Why can a farmer in Punjab grow rice, which needs 100 cm of rain, in a region of low rainfall? What does this tell us about the relationship between crops and climate?

Model answer

Because a dense network of canal irrigation and tube-wells supplies water, so rainfall is no longer the limiting factor. This shows that technology can modify the geographical conditions a crop needs — but at a cost: groundwater depletion and, in some areas, water logging and salinity. Climate still sets limits, but irrigation, HYV seeds and fertilisers shift them. (Model answer.)

2.

A district wants to increase farmers’ income without expanding cropland. Suggest a plan using this chapter.

Model answer

(i) Shift to higher-value crops — horticulture (fruits and vegetables), plantation crops, oilseeds — since India is already a leading producer. (ii) Grow pulses in rotation to restore fertility and cut fertiliser cost. (iii) Use HYV seeds, crop insurance, KCC credit and MSP information to reduce risk and exploitation by middlemen. (iv) Improve transport and processing links so that produce reaches markets fresh, as plantations require. (v) Adopt water-efficient irrigation to protect the resource base. (Model answer.)

3.

“Plantation agriculture is agriculture and industry at once.” Explain.

Model answer

Because a plantation grows a single crop over a large area using capital-intensive inputs and migrant labour — that is agriculture — and all the produce is used as raw material in the respective industries, with processing often done on the estate (as with tea, processed within the garden to restore freshness). It therefore needs a well-developed network of transport and communication connecting plantation areas, processing industries and markets. (Model answer.)

4.

Why did land reform laws not achieve what they intended? What does the chapter suggest about the gap between law and implementation?

Model answer

The chapter says the laws of land reform were enacted but implementation was lacking or lukewarm. Holdings remained fragmented because of the right of inheritance, and zamindari abolition and consolidation did not reach all regions. Later strategies — the Green Revolution and White Revolution — improved production but concentrated development in a few areas. The lesson is that institutional change requires political will and local participation, not only legislation. (Model answer.)

5.

Compare the Bhoodan–Gramdan approach with government land reform. Which is likely to work faster, and which more fairly?

Model answer

Bhoodan–Gramdan was voluntary: individuals and zamindars gifted land or whole villages, motivated by Vinoba Bhave’s appeal, Gandhian ideals and, in part, fear of the land ceiling act. It was quick where goodwill existed, but depended on the generosity of a few and could not be enforced. Government land reform was legal and universal but suffered from lukewarm implementation. Voluntary transfer builds consent; legal reform is enforceable but slower. Ideally the two work together. (Model answer.)

6.

India is the largest producer of pulses yet imports them. Using the chapter, suggest what should change.

Model answer

Pulses need less moisture, survive dry conditions and restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen, so they are ideal for rain-fed and dry regions and for rotation. What is needed is wider adoption in rotation, assured procurement and MSP so farmers do not shift to more profitable cereals, better seed supply, and inclusion in irrigation and insurance schemes. Since pulses are the main protein source in a vegetarian diet, raising their production reduces both import dependence and soil degradation. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Basics

  • Two-thirds of the population in agriculture; primary activity; >60% livelihood.
  • Raw material for industry; exports tea, coffee, spices.

Farming types

  • Primitive subsistence: small patches, hoe/dao/digging sticks, slash and burn, low productivity.
  • Names: jhumming, Pamlou, Dipa, Bewar/Dahiya, Podu/Penda, Pama Dabi/Koman/Bringa, Kumari, Valre/Waltre, Khil, Kuruwa.
  • World: Milpa, Conuco, Roca, Masole, Ladang, Ray.
  • Intensive subsistence: labour-intensive, high population pressure, right of inheritance.
  • Commercial: HYV, fertilisers, insecticides, pesticides; plantation = single crop, capital-intensive, migrant labour.

Seasons

  • Rabi: Oct–Dec to Apr–Jun (wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard).
  • Kharif: monsoon to Sep–Oct (paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut, soyabean).
  • Zaid: summer, between the two (watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder). Sugarcane: almost a year.
  • Aus, Aman, Boro: three paddy crops in Assam, West Bengal, Odisha.

Crops and conditions

  • Rice: >25°C, >100 cm, kharif; second after China.
  • Wheat: cool season, bright ripening sun, 50–75 cm, rabi; Ganga–Satluj and Deccan black soil.
  • Millets: jowar (3rd food crop), bajra (sandy/shallow black), ragi (dry regions, iron and calcium).
  • Maize: 21–27°C, old alluvial, food and fodder.
  • Pulses: largest producer and consumer; protein; nitrogen fixation except arhar.
  • Sugarcane: 21–27°C, 75–100 cm; second after Brazil.
  • Oilseeds: 12% of cropped area; groundnut half; Gujarat first (2019–20).
  • Tea: plantation, labour-intensive, processed in the garden; Assam, Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri, TN, Kerala.
  • Coffee: Arabica from Yemen, Baba Budan Hills, Nilgiri.
  • Horticulture: second in fruits and vegetables (2020).
  • Fibres: cotton (black soil, 210 frost-free days, 6–8 months), jute (golden fibre), hemp, silk (sericulture).

Reforms

  • Land reform in the First Five Year Plan; collectivisation, consolidation, cooperation, abolition of zamindari.
  • Green Revolution (1960s–70s) + White Revolution (Operation Flood).
  • 1980s–90s: crop insurance, Grameen banks, cooperative societies, KCC, PAIS, weather bulletins, MSP.

Bhoodan–Gramdan

  • Vinoba Bhave; Pochampally, Telangana; Ram Chandra Reddy, 80 acres for 80 villagers.
  • Gramdan = gift of villages; land ceiling act; Blood-less Revolution.

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Agriculture is a primary activity: two-thirds of India’s people are engaged in it, it produces most of our food and raw material for industry, and it supports the livelihood of more than 60 per cent of the population. Farming ranges from primitive subsistence — slash and burn cultivation known as jhumming, Pamlou, Dipa, Podu, Bewar, Kumari, Khil and Kuruwa in different regions — through labour-intensive intensive subsistence farming, to commercial farming with HYV seeds, fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides, of which plantation agriculture is a special type.

India has three cropping seasons: rabi (sown October–December, harvested April–June), kharif (with the monsoon, harvested September–October) and the short summer zaid season. The major crops are rice, wheat, millets, maize, pulses, sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee, horticultural crops, and the fibre crops cotton, jute, hemp and silk, each with its own soil, temperature, rainfall and producing states. India is the largest producer of pulses and second in rice, sugarcane, groundnut, tea, cotton and fruits and vegetables.

After Independence the state pursued institutional reform — collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari — with land reform as the focus of the First Five Year Plan. The Green Revolution and White Revolution followed in the 1960s and 1970s, and since the 1980s a comprehensive land development programme has added crop insurance, rural banks, KCC, PAIS, weather bulletins and minimum support prices. Alongside, Vinoba Bhave’s Bhoodan–Gramdan movement sought voluntary redistribution of land — the “blood-less revolution”.
